title: What are Flink SQL catalogs (HiveCatalog, JdbcCatalog, in-memory default catalog), how do they store table metadata persistently, and why are they important for production (table definitions survive job restarts, shared across teams)?
shortTitle: What are Flink SQL catalogs and why are they important for production
keyPoints: A Flink SQL catalog stores metadata for databases, tables, views, and functions in a three-level namespace.
The default GenericInMemoryCatalog loses all definitions when the session exits or the job restarts.
HiveCatalog persists metadata in a Hive Metastore backed by a relational database, surviving restarts.
JdbcCatalog automatically exposes a live relational database's tables as Flink tables without DDL.
Persistent catalogs enable table sharing across teams so definitions are created once and reused everywhere.
Catalogs are the backbone of metadata governance: access control, lineage, and discovery depend on them.
Modern deployments use lakehouse catalogs like Iceberg or Paimon for full table-format integration.

s1_definition.oneliner: A Flink SQL catalog is the metadata store for tables and functions; the in-memory one forgets on restart, while HiveCatalog and JdbcCatalog persist and share definitions across jobs and teams.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Catalog** – The metadata store holding databases, tables, views, and functions in a three-level namespace: catalog.database.object.
- **GenericInMemoryCatalog** – The default catalog that keeps definitions in session memory, lost on restart.
- **HiveCatalog** – Persists metadata in a Hive Metastore backed by a relational database, making definitions durable and shared.
- **JdbcCatalog** – Connects to a relational database and exposes its real tables as Flink tables automatically.
- **Governance** – Persistent catalogs enable access control, lineage tracking, and cross-team table sharing.
s1_definition.analogy: When the National Bank of India writes SQL against its transaction streams, every table needs a definition. The default in-memory catalog is like writing those definitions on a whiteboard: the moment the room is cleared, they are gone. A HiveCatalog is like storing them in a shared central register that every department can read, so the accounts table defined by the payments team is instantly usable by the fraud team and survives overnight reboots.

```text
  InMemory vs HiveCatalog Lifecycle

  InMemory:                     HiveCatalog:
  ┌──────────┐                 ┌──────────┐
  │ Session   │                 │ Session   │
  │ starts    │                 │ starts    │
  │ CREATE TBL│                 │ CREATE TBL│──▶ Hive Metastore
  │ (in heap) │                 │ (stored)  │    (MySQL backend)
  └─────┬────┘                 └─────┬────┘
        │ restart                     │ restart
        ▼                             ▼
  ┌──────────┐                 ┌──────────┐
  │ Session   │                 │ Session   │
  │ starts    │                 │ starts    │
  │ TABLE GONE│                 │ TABLE     │◀── Hive Metastore
  │ must redo │                 │ STILL HERE│    (still has it)
  └──────────┘                 └──────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A Flink SQL catalog stores the definitions of databases, tables, views, and functions in a three-level namespace. The default GenericInMemoryCatalog keeps everything in the session's heap, so definitions vanish on restart. HiveCatalog persists metadata in a Hive Metastore backed by a relational database, making definitions durable and shared across all sessions. JdbcCatalog connects to a live database and automatically exposes its tables without any DDL.

Catalogs matter for production because they are the backbone of metadata governance. Without a persistent catalog, every job must re-run DDL after a restart, definitions drift between teams, and there is no single source of truth. With HiveCatalog, one team defines the transactions table once and every other team queries it immediately.

At the National Bank of India, payments, fraud, and reporting teams all needed the same core tables. Early on, each team redefined them in their own in-memory session, so definitions drifted and every restart wiped them out. We moved to HiveCatalog backed by a shared metastore, and definitions survived every restart while all teams shared a single source of truth.

Remember one sentence: use a persistent catalog like HiveCatalog so table definitions survive restarts and are shared across teams, because the in-memory catalog loses everything when the session exits.
